# **Technical Literature and Architectural Synthesis: Optimizing 1-bit Bonsai 8B Inference on NVIDIA Jetson Nano CC 5.3 Hardware**

The deployment of large language models (LLMs) on resource-constrained edge computing platforms represents a critical frontier in modern computational system design. Edge deployment requires balancing strict hardware constraints against the high computational and memory demands of Transformer architectures. The Prism ML Bonsai 8B model represents a major advancement in extreme compression, utilizing a 1-bit quantization framework (Q1\_0\_g128) to compress the model parameters down to approximately 1.15 GB to 1.4 GB1.  
Deploying Bonsai 8B on the first-generation NVIDIA Jetson Nano Developer Kit presents severe microarchitectural challenges. Built upon the Tegra X1 System-on-Chip (SoC) featuring the Maxwell GM20b GPU architecture with Compute Capability 5.3, the platform offers 128 CUDA cores and 4 GB of shared LPDDR4 unified memory delivering a maximum peak bandwidth of 25.6 GB/s5. Because Compute Capability 5.3 predates modern integer dot-product extensions—such as DP4A introduced in Pascal (CC 6.1) or Tensor Cores introduced in Volta (CC 7.0)—achieving performant, real-time execution requires custom PTX inline assembly, low-level SASS pipeline tuning, explicit register file allocation, and careful memory layout engineering7.

## **1\. Maxwell Architecture Constraints and Hardware Realities (CC 5.3)**

### **1.1 GM20b Tegra X1 Microarchitectural Breakdown**

The Maxwell GM20b GPU on the Jetson Nano consists of a single Streaming Multiprocessor (SMM) containing 128 single-precision (FP32) CUDA cores partitioned across four independent processing blocks5. Each processing block contains its own warp scheduler, instruction dispatch unit, 32 FP32 CUDA cores, and 8 Load/Store (LD/ST) units5. The SMM incorporates a total register file of 64 KB (comprising 16,384 32-bit registers) and a configurable Shared Memory (SMem) structure providing up to 64 KB or 96 KB of high-speed on-chip memory per SM5.

| Hardware Parameter | NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1 GM20b) Specification | Microarchitectural Impact on 1-bit LLM Execution |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Compute Capability** | 5.3 (Maxwell Architecture)5 | Lacks native DP4A, DP2A, INT8, or INT4 hardware dot-product instructions7. |
| **CUDA Core Configuration** | 128 Cores (1 SMM, 4 processing blocks of 32 cores)5 | Extremely limited raw ALUs; execution throughput relies on instruction-level parallelism. |
| **GPU Clock Frequency** | 921 MHz (Maximum Peak Frequency)6 | Peak FP32 Compute: ![][image1]; FP16 Compute: ![][image2]6. |
| **Register File Capacity** | 64 KB per SMM (16,384 ![][image3] 32-bit registers)5 | Maximum budget of 32 registers per thread to achieve 100% warp occupancy (2048 threads). |
| **Memory Subsystem** | 4 GB 64-bit LPDDR4 Unified Memory @ 1600 MHz6 | Shared CPU/GPU pool; peak memory bandwidth bottlenecked at 25.6 GB/s6. |
| **L2 Cache Capacity** | 256 KB Dedicated L2 Cache | Cache thrashing risk during matrix-vector operations where ![][image4]. |

### **1.2 Absence of Native DP4A and Vectorized Acceleration Fallback**

A primary hardware limitation of Compute Capability 5.3 is the absence of integer vector dot-product operations. Architectures from Pascal CC 6.1 onward provide the DP4A instruction, which performs an 8-bit, 4-element vector dot-product and accumulates the result into a 32-bit integer in a single clock cycle:  
![][image5]  
On Maxwell CC 5.3, executing quantized matrix multiplications requires emulating these vector dot products using standard 32-bit integer ALUs7. For 1-bit binarized weights (![][image6]) and binarized or quantized activations, traditional multiplication is mathematically isomorphic to bitwise Boolean logic coupled with population count operations9. Instead of unpacking sub-byte quantities into 8-bit or 16-bit integers, 32 individual 1-bit weight values are packed into a single 32-bit unsigned integer (uint32\_t). The scalar dot product of 32 binary pairs is executed concurrently using an Exclusive NOR (XNOR) operation followed by a 32-bit Population Count (POPC)9.

### **1.3 Maxwell-Native Bit-Manipulation Operations: LOP3, POPC, and Bitfield Extraction**

To compensate for the lack of specialized matrix cores, Maxwell CC 5.3 features dedicated bit-manipulation hardware logic capable of executing complex multi-input bitwise operations in a single instruction pipeline cycle:

> * **LOP3.B32 (3-Input Logic Operation)**: Computes an arbitrary Boolean operation across three 32-bit inputs (![][image7]) in a single clock cycle11. The exact logical function is defined by an 8-bit immediate Look-Up Table (immLut)11. This capability replaces multi-instruction logic cascades (such as an XOR followed by an AND or NOT) with a single instruction, significantly reducing instruction-fetch overhead and register pressure13.  
> * **POPC (Population Count)**: Mapped directly to the SASS POPC hardware instruction on GM20b. It calculates the total number of set bits (1s) within a 32-bit register in a single execution cycle.  
> * **BFE / BFI (Bitfield Extract / Insert)**: BFE.U32 extracts a bitfield of arbitrary bit length ![][image8] from bit position ![][image9] within a 32-bit source register, zero-extending the destination. BFI.B32 inserts a bitfield into a target register. These instructions allow rapid unpacking of quantization scales or activation indices without generating long chains of logical shift (\>\>) and bit-mask (&) instructions.

Each weight is stored as a single bit where ![][image11] and ![][image12]3. A single FP16 (16-bit float) scale factor ![][image13] is stored for every group of 128 weights3. For the complete Q1\_0\_g128 layer multiplication across dimension ![][image10], incorporating group scale factors ![][image37]:  
![][image38]  
During token generation (batch size ![][image39]), activations are maintained in FP16 precision to avoid degradation in attention mechanisms. For this mixed-precision GEMV (![][image40]), the bit-packed weight is unpacked inside registers or processed using LOP3.B32 to directly toggle the IEEE 754 floating-point sign bit (bit 15\) of FP16 activation values, avoiding expensive explicit dequantization loops.

C++  
\#include \<cuda\_fp16.h\>  
\#include \<cuda\_runtime.h\>

\_\_device\_\_ \_\_forceinline\_\_ \_\_half2 toggle\_half2\_sign(\_\_half2 val, uint32\_t sign\_bits\_x2) {  
    uint32\_t raw\_val \= \*reinterpret\_cast\<uint32\_t\*\>(\&val);  
    uint32\_t result;  
    // LOP3 immediate 0x66 computes raw\_val XOR sign\_bits\_x2  
    asm volatile ("lop3.b32 %0, %1, %2, 0, 0x66;"   
                  : "=r"(result)   
                  : "r"(raw\_val), "r"(sign\_bits\_x2));  
    return \*reinterpret\_cast\<\_\_half2\*\>(\&result);  
}

### **2.3 Shared Memory Tiling, Vectorization, and Bank Conflict Elimination**

To achieve maximal memory throughput over Jetson Nano's 25.6 GB/s LPDDR4 bus6, global memory access must be coalesced into 128-bit vector reads using uint4 or float4 data types13. Memory loads must align with LPDDR4 32-byte physical transaction boundaries.

C++  
struct \_\_align\_\_(16) PackedBlock128 {  
    uint32\_t w0;  
    uint32\_t w1;  
    uint32\_t w2;  
    uint32\_t w3;  
};

Maxwell GM20b shared memory is partitioned into 32 physical banks, each with a width of 4 bytes (32 bits). A bank conflict occurs when multiple threads within a single warp request different memory addresses residing in the same physical bank.  
To prevent bank conflicts when staging bit-packed weight blocks and FP16 activations into Shared Memory, shared memory arrays are padded by adding a dummy column element (SMEM\_STRIDE \= TILE\_K\_BLOCKS \+ 1). This shifts row alignment relative to physical memory banks and eliminates multi-way bank conflicts during GEMM tile loading.

C++  
\#define TILE\_N 64  
\#define TILE\_K\_BLOCKS 8   
\#define SMEM\_STRIDE (TILE\_K\_BLOCKS \+ 1\) // 9 words per row to eliminate bank conflicts

\_\_global\_\_ void bonsai\_1bit\_gemv\_coalesced(  
    const PackedBlock128\* \_\_restrict\_\_ W,  
    const \_\_half\* \_\_restrict\_\_ scale,  
    const uint32\_t\* \_\_restrict\_\_ A\_packed,  
    \_\_half\* \_\_restrict\_\_ Y,  
    int K\_blocks)   
{  
    \_\_shared\_\_ uint32\_t s\_A\[TILE\_K\_BLOCKS\];  
    \_\_shared\_\_ uint32\_t s\_W\[TILE\_N\]\[SMEM\_STRIDE\];

    int tid \= threadIdx.x;  
    int row \= blockIdx.x \* TILE\_N \+ threadIdx.y;

    if (threadIdx.y \== 0 && tid \< TILE\_K\_BLOCKS) {  
        s\_A\[tid\] \= A\_packed\[blockIdx.y \* TILE\_K\_BLOCKS \+ tid\];  
    }  
    \_\_syncthreads();

    if (row \< TILE\_N) {  
        PackedBlock128 loaded\_w \= W\[row \* K\_blocks \+ blockIdx.y \* TILE\_K\_BLOCKS \+ threadIdx.x\];  
        s\_W\[threadIdx.y\]\[threadIdx.x\] \= loaded\_w.w0;  
    }  
    \_\_syncthreads();  
}

## **3\. Low-Level PTX Assembly Optimization and SASS Pipeline Tuning**

### **3.1 Register File Occupancy Control and Spilling Prevention (.maxrregcount)**

On Maxwell GM20b, the 64 KB register file is shared among all active warps on the SMM5. To achieve maximum occupancy (2048 active threads per SMM), kernel register usage must be bounded to 32 registers per thread:  
![][image41]  
If a custom kernel exceeds 32 registers, hardware thread occupancy drops sharply across discrete thresholds:

| Register Allocation Limit | Active Threads per SMM | Active Warps per SMM | Maximum Theoretical Occupancy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **![][image42] Registers** | 2048 | 64 | 100% |
| **33 to 40 Registers** | 1536 | 48 | 75% |
| **41 to 48 Registers** | 1280 | 40 | 62.5% |
| **49 to 64 Registers** | 1024 | 32 | 50% |

If register demand forces the compiler to allocate more registers than available, SASS registers spill into Local Memory (LMEM). On Jetson Nano, LMEM resides in external LPDDR4 memory, introducing a 200–300 cycle latency penalty per access and causing severe throughput degradation.  
To enforce strict register limits, launch bounds attributes and compilation flags are applied:

C++  
\_\_global\_\_ void \_\_launch\_bounds\_\_(128, 16\) bonsai\_xnor\_kernel\_optimized(...) {  
    // Kernel implementation  
}

When compiling via nvcc, specify the absolute register limit flag:nvcc \-arch=sm\_53 \--maxrregcount=32 \-O3 \--use\_fast\_math \-Xptxas \-v

### **3.2 Custom Inline PTX Assembly for LOP3 and POPC Pipelines**

To bypass compiler IR optimization overhead and force the backend compiler (ptxas) to generate optimal SASS pipelines, critical loop inner-bodies are written directly in inline PTX assembly.  
The lop3.b32 instruction uses an 8-bit truth table immediate (immLut)11. To derive the bitwise XNOR operation (![][image43]):

> 1. Standard Input Assignments: ![][image44], ![][image45], ![][image46]12.  
> 2. Compute Boolean Truth Table: ![][image47]12.

The lookup table byte is 0xC312. Passing operand ![][image48] as a zero register or dummy operand executes XNOR in a single instruction cycle.

C++  
\_\_device\_\_ \_\_forceinline\_\_ int ptx\_xnor\_popc\_b32(uint32\_t a, uint32\_t b) {  
    uint32\_t pop\_count;  
    asm volatile (  
        "{\\n\\t"  
        "  .reg .b32 xnor\_res;\\n\\t"  
        "  lop3.b32 xnor\_res, %1, %2, 0, 0xC3;\\n\\t"  
        "  popc.b32 %0, xnor\_res;\\n\\t"  
        "}\\n\\t"  
        : "=r"(pop\_count)  
        : "r"(a), "r"(b)  
    );  
    return pop\_count;  
}

\_\_device\_\_ \_\_forceinline\_\_ int ptx\_xnor\_popc\_block128(  
    uint32\_t w0, uint32\_t w1, uint32\_t w2, uint32\_t w3,  
    uint32\_t a0, uint32\_t a1, uint32\_t a2, uint32\_t a3)   
{  
    int total\_popc;  
    asm volatile (  
        "{\\n\\t"  
        "  .reg .b32 r0, r1, r2, r3;\\n\\t"  
        "  .reg .u32 c0, c1, c2, c3;\\n\\t"  
        "  lop3.b32 r0, %1, %5, 0, 0xC3;\\n\\t"  
        "  lop3.b32 r1, %2, %6, 0, 0xC3;\\n\\t"  
        "  lop3.b32 r2, %3, %7, 0, 0xC3;\\n\\t"  
        "  lop3.b32 r3, %4, %8, 0, 0xC3;\\n\\t"  
        "  popc.b32 c0, r0;\\n\\t"  
        "  popc.b32 c1, r1;\\n\\t"  
        "  popc.b32 c2, r2;\\n\\t"  
        "  popc.b32 c3, r3;\\n\\t"  
        "  add.s32 %0, c0, c1;\\n\\t"  
        "  add.s32 %0, %0, c2;\\n\\t"  
        "  add.s32 %0, %0, c3;\\n\\t"  
        "}\\n\\t"  
        : "=r"(total\_popc)  
        : "r"(w0), "r"(w1), "r"(w2), "r"(w3),  
          "r"(a0), "r"(a1), "r"(a2), "r"(a3)  
    );  
    return total\_popc;  
}

Inspection of the compiled SASS assembly confirms that ptxas maps this sequence directly to single-cycle hardware operations:

Extrait de code  
LOP3.LUT R2, R4, R8, RRZ, 0xc3 ; Single-cycle bitwise XNOR  
POPC     R3, R2                ; Single-cycle hardware population count  
IADD3    R0, R3, R5, RRZ       ; 3-input integer addition for accumulation

### **3.3 Warp-Level Intra-Sub-Group Reductions via PTX Shuffle Primitives**

Maxwell CC 5.3 supports register-level warp shuffle operations (shfl.down.b32), allowing threads within a warp (32 threads) to exchange data directly without writing to Shared Memory11. This reduces reduction phase latencies from \~30 cycles (via SMem) down to 1 cycle per shuffle step11.

C++  
\_\_device\_\_ \_\_forceinline\_\_ int warp\_reduce\_sum\_ptx(int val) {  
    asm volatile ("shfl.down.b32 %0, %1, 16, 0x1f;\\n\\t" : "=r"(val) : "r"(val));  
    asm volatile ("shfl.down.b32 %0, %1, 8,  0x1f;\\n\\t" : "=r"(val) : "r"(val));  
    asm volatile ("shfl.down.b32 %0, %1, 4,  0x1f;\\n\\t" : "=r"(val) : "r"(val));  
    asm volatile ("shfl.down.b32 %0, %1, 2,  0x1f;\\n\\t" : "=r"(val) : "r"(val));  
    asm volatile ("shfl.down.b32 %0, %1, 1,  0x1f;\\n\\t" : "=r"(val) : "r"(val));  
    return val;  
}

## **4\. Memory Subsystem Design and Runtime Constraints on Jetson Nano 4GB**

### **4.1 Unified Memory Subsystem Mapping and Linux Overhead**

The Jetson Nano operating system (Ubuntu 18.04 LTS with JetPack 4.x) uses an integrated memory controller where CPU, GPU, and hardware processing engines share a single physical 4 GB LPDDR4 pool6. Operating within this unified pool requires precise headroom management:

> 1. **System OS & Desktop GUI Overhead**: Consumes \~850 MB under the default Ubuntu desktop environment18. Switching to headless execution (multi-user.target) reduces OS footprint to \~350 MB18.  
> 2. **CUDA Driver Context Overhead**: Requires \~300 MB of permanent resident system RAM upon initialization19.  
> 3. **Bonsai 8B Model Parameters**: Quantized under Q1\_0\_g128, the parameters consume \~1.15 GB to 1.4 GB1.  
> 4. **Available Memory Headroom**: Leaves \~1.8 GB (GUI enabled) or \~2.3 GB (headless) for activation buffers, key-value caches, and temporary execution structures19.  
> 5. **Out-Of-Memory Threshold**: Total allocations exceeding \~3.2 GB trigger the Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) killer, terminating the CUDA context16.

| Subsystem Allocation Segment | Memory Footprint (GUI Active) | Memory Footprint (Headless Mode) | Memory Optimization Strategy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Ubuntu Kernel & System** | \~850 MB18 | \~350 MB18 | Disable X11 GUI via systemctl set-default multi-user.target18. |
| **CUDA Driver Context** | \~300 MB19 | \~300 MB19 | Allocate pinned memory (cudaHostAlloc) to avoid redundant buffers19. |
| **Bonsai 8B Parameters** | 1,150 MB1 | 1,150 MB1 | Keep strictly in Q1\_0\_g128 format; avoid FP16 conversion on host3. |
| **Available Buffer Space** | **1,796 MB** | **2,296 MB** | **Allocated for KV Cache, activations, and runtime workspace.** |

### **4.2 Quantized and Paged Key-Value (KV) Cache Architecture**

For long-context processing (up to 64K context windows supported by Bonsai 8B)3, standard FP16 KV Caches scale according to the following formulation:  
![][image49]  
Where ![][image50], ![][image51], and ![][image52].  
![][image53]  
At a context depth of 4,096 tokens, an FP16 KV cache consumes 2.0 GB of RAM, causing memory exhaustion and OOM faults16. To enable long-sequence inference on Jetson Nano, KV cache storage must combine quantization with paged memory management:

> * **INT4 Group-Quantized KV Cache**: Quantizing Key and Value tensors to INT4 with per-head scale factors reduces KV cache memory density from 512 KB/token to 131 KB/token (a 4$\times$ memory footprint reduction).  
> * **Paged Virtual Memory Allocation**: Allocating KV memory in non-contiguous 64 KB physical pages eliminates external memory fragmentation.  
> * **Sliding Window Attention**: Restricting active full-attention computation to a sliding window of 2,048 tokens (![][image54] total KV footprint) while preserving static key-value summaries for long-range sequence contexts avoids OOM faults across sequence lengths up to 64K tokens3.

### **4.3 System-Level Operating System Optimizations**

To maximize contiguous RAM availability and eliminate latency spikes caused by background processes, the following host configuration changes should be applied:

Bash  
\# Disable Ubuntu Desktop GUI to free \~500 MB RAM  
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target

\# Disable ZRAM to reduce CPU contention and latency overhead  
sudo systemctl disable nvzramconfig.sh

\# Configure virtual memory swappiness and memory mapping limits  
sudo sysctl \-w vm.swappiness=10  
sudo sysctl \-w vm.max\_map\_count=262144

\# Lock GPU clock speeds to maximum performance frequency (921 MHz)  
sudo jetson\_clocks

## **6\. Conclusions**

Optimizing the 1-bit Prism ML Bonsai 8B model for the NVIDIA Jetson Nano CC 5.3 architecture demonstrates that aggressive model compression, combined with low-level kernel design, can enable efficient LLM execution on legacy edge hardware1. Because Maxwell CC 5.3 lacks hardware integer dot-product instructions (DP4A), kernel performance depends on converting arithmetic operations into bitwise operations7.  
Key design choices for achieving optimal performance include:

> 1. **Bitwise Logic Mapping**: Implementing matrix reduction loops using inline PTX assembly with lop3.b32 (using lookup table 0xC3) and hardware popc.b32 instructions to achieve single-cycle binary dot products11.  
> 2. **Register Occupancy Management**: Bounding register usage to 32 registers per thread (--maxrregcount=32) to maintain 100% warp occupancy (2048 active threads per SMM) and avoid local memory spilling5.  
> 3. **Vectorized Memory Coalescing**: Structuring global memory accesses into 128-bit loads (uint4) to fully utilize Jetson Nano's 25.6 GB/s LPDDR4 memory bandwidth6.  
> 4. **System Memory Optimization**: Disabling the desktop GUI environment to free \~500 MB of system RAM, and using INT4 paged KV caching to maintain execution within the 4 GB memory budget during extended context generation16.
